html:
The Silk Road opened in the second century BCE, when envoys of China's Han dynasty reached Central Asia and the Chinese state began to push its trade and power westward. The overland routes that grew from this linked China to Iran, India and the Mediterranean for some 1,500 years.

It began with a mission. Around 138 BCE Emperor Wu sent Zhang Qian west to find allies against the Xiongnu, the nomad empire to China's north. The Xiongnu held him captive for about ten years. He escaped, reached the Yuezhi, who had settled in Bactria, and came home around 125 BCE with news of rich lands in the west and their fine horses.

The Han then pushed armies and garrisons along the Gansu corridor and into the oasis cities of the Tarim basin, protecting the route.

The "road" was really a web of caravan routes, and few traders went the whole way:

  • Chinese silk went west through many hands, through the Parthian Empire to the Roman Empire, where it became a luxury.
  • Horses, glass, silver, wool and spices went east.
  • Sogdian merchants from around Samarkand became the great middlemen, as their letters show.

Ideas and faiths travelled along it too. Buddhism reached China this way, and later Manichaeism, Christianity and Islam spread east, while papermaking went west. The name "Silk Road" was coined only in the nineteenth century by a German geographer. The routes declined in the fifteenth century as sea trade took over.
